subject: Economy
sub_topic: SEBI — Securities and Exchange Board of India

concepts.name: SEBI's Establishment: Statutory vs. Non-Statutory Phase
key_dimensions: SEBI was first set up as a non-statutory body in 1988 under a government resolution
Granted statutory status via the SEBI Act, 1992 — a common UPSC trap on the year
Distinction between establishment date (1988) and statutory empowerment (1992)
Triggered by the Harshad Mehta scam context — examiner often links cause and effect

concepts.name: SEBI's Tri-Functional Mandate: Quasi-Legislative, Quasi-Executive, and Quasi-Judicial Powers
key_dimensions: Quasi-legislative: Power to frame regulations under Section 30 of SEBI Act
Quasi-executive: Power to investigate, conduct inspections, and enforce compliance
Quasi-judicial: Power to adjudicate disputes, issue cease-and-desist orders, and impose penalties
UPSC trap: Unlike a pure regulator, SEBI combines all three powers — distinguish from CCI or TRAI

concepts.name: SEBI's Organizational Structure and Composition
key_dimensions: Board consists of a Chairman + 9 members (mix of whole-time and part-time)
Chairman appointed by the Central Government — not independent appointment
Two members from the Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Law (ex-officio) — reduces full autonomy
UPSC trap: SEBI is not fully independent; government nominees sit on the board, unlike RBI's structure

concepts.name: SEBI's Triple Role: Protector, Regulator, and Developer
key_dimensions: Investor protection: Redressal mechanisms, SCORES portal, disclosure norms
Market regulation: Oversight of intermediaries, exchanges, and listed companies
Market development: Introducing new instruments (REITs, InvITs, SME platforms)
UPSC trap: Development role is often ignored — SEBI actively promotes market depth, not just polices it

concepts.name: SEBI's Jurisdiction: Securities It Regulates vs. Does Not Regulate
key_dimensions: Regulates: Equity, debentures, mutual funds, derivatives, collective investment schemes
Does NOT regulate: Chit funds (state subject), insurance (IRDAI), bank deposits (RBI)
Commodity derivatives: Jurisdiction merged from FMC to SEBI in 2015 — a high-yield recent change
UPSC trap: Government securities and currency derivatives involve RBI–SEBI overlap — must know boundary

concepts.name: SEBI vs. RBI: Regulatory Overlap in Debt and Forex Markets
key_dimensions: Corporate bonds and non-convertible debentures: SEBI's domain
Government securities (G-Secs): RBI's domain under RBI Act
Currency derivatives: Jointly regulated — RBI sets policy limits, SEBI oversees exchange mechanism
UPSC trap: External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) fall under RBI, not SEBI — frequently confused

concepts.name: Insider Trading Regulations: Definition, Prohibition, and UPDI
key_dimensions: SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 — replaced 1992 regulations
Definition of 'insider' expanded to include connected persons with unpublished price-sensitive information (UPSI)
UPSI includes financial results, mergers, dividend declarations — specific list is examinable
Legitimate defenses: Trading plans pre-filed with stock exchanges; contra-trade restrictions

concepts.name: SEBI's Enforcement Powers: Penalties, Disgorgement, and Debarment
key_dimensions: Monetary penalties up to ₹25 crore or 3 times the profit made — whichever is higher (post-2014 amendment)
Disgorgement: Recovery of illegal gains — distinct from penalty, used in addition to it
Debarment: Banning individuals/entities from securities markets for specified periods
UPSC trap: SEBI cannot impose criminal penalties directly — criminal prosecution routed through courts

concepts.name: Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT): Jurisdiction and Limitations
key_dimensions: SAT hears appeals against SEBI orders — established under Chapter VIA of SEBI Act
Presided over by a retired High Court judge or Supreme Court judge
Appeals from SAT lie directly to the Supreme Court (not High Court) — a classic UPSC trap
SAT also hears appeals against IRDAI and PFRDA orders — multi-regulator appellate body

concepts.name: Collective Investment Schemes (CIS): SEBI's Special Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Any scheme pooling ≥100 investors and corpus ≥₹20 crore requires SEBI registration as CIS
Landmark cases: Sahara case — Supreme Court upheld SEBI's jurisdiction over Optionally Fully Convertible Debentures
Ponzi-adjacent schemes (plantation, emu farming) brought under CIS ambit to protect investors
UPSC trap: Chit funds are explicitly excluded from CIS under SEBI Act — regulated by states under Chit Funds Act, 1982

concepts.name: SEBI and Mutual Funds: Regulatory Framework and Categorization
key_dimensions: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 — all mutual funds must register with SEBI
2017–18 categorization reform: SEBI mandated uniform categories (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap) to prevent overlap
Expense ratio caps: SEBI periodically revises TER (Total Expense Ratio) limits — reduces cost to investors
UPSC trap: AMFI (Association of Mutual Funds in India) is a self-regulatory body, NOT a statutory regulator — SEBI regulates, AMFI facilitates

concepts.name: SEBI's Role in IPO Regulation: Disclosure Norms and DRHP
key_dimensions: Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP) must be filed with SEBI before any public issue
SEBI does not 'approve' an IPO — it only reviews disclosures; investors must conduct own due diligence
Pricing: Book-building vs. fixed-price method — both permitted under SEBI framework
UPSC trap: SEBI's observation letter ≠ approval or guarantee of company quality — a frequent misconception tested

concepts.name: Takeover Code: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
key_dimensions: Trigger threshold: Acquiring 25% or more of shares/voting rights triggers mandatory open offer
Open offer size: Must be for at least 26% of total shares from public shareholders
Creeping acquisition: Up to 5% additional shares per financial year allowed without open offer (between 25–75% holding)
UPSC trap: The 25% trigger replaced the earlier 15% threshold under 1997 regulations — year and threshold often tested

concepts.name: Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs): SEBI's Three-Category Framework
key_dimensions: Category I: Venture capital, SME funds, social venture funds — get tax/regulatory incentives
Category II: Private equity, debt funds — no specific incentives or restrictions
Category III: Hedge funds, PIPE funds — can use leverage and complex trading strategies
UPSC trap: FPIs and AIFs are often confused — FPIs are foreign investors; AIFs are domestic pooled vehicles

concepts.name: REITs and InvITs: SEBI as Regulator of Hybrid Investment Instruments
key_dimensions: Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) — regulated under SEBI since 2014
Must distribute at least 90% of net distributable cash flows to unit holders
Listed on stock exchanges — blend of debt-like income and equity-like tradability
UPSC trap: REITs invest in completed, revenue-generating real estate — NOT under-construction projects; InvITs cover infrastructure assets like roads, power lines

concepts.name: SCORES Platform and Investor Grievance Redressal Mechanism
key_dimensions: SCORES: SEBI Complaints Redress System — centralized web-based grievance platform
Complaints must be first lodged with the entity; if unresolved, escalated to SEBI via SCORES
Time-bound resolution: Intermediaries must respond within 30 days
UPSC trap: SCORES handles securities market grievances only — banking or insurance complaints go to RBI Ombudsman or IRDAI Bima Bharosa respectively

concepts.name: SEBI's Role in Corporate Governance: LODR Regulations
key_dimensions: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 — replaced Listing Agreement
Mandates: Independent directors, audit committees, related-party transaction disclosures, board diversity
SEBI enforces corporate governance for listed companies; MCA governs unlisted companies under Companies Act
UPSC trap: SEBI and MCA have overlapping jurisdiction on listed companies — both can act, but SEBI's LODR is primary for disclosure

concepts.name: SEBI's International Linkages: IOSCO Membership and Cross-Border Regulation
key_dimensions: SEBI is a member of IOSCO (International Organization of Securities Commissions) — the global standard-setter for securities regulation
Signatory to IOSCO's Multilateral MoU (MMoU) — enables cross-border information sharing on market manipulation
SEBI signs bilateral MoUs with foreign regulators (e.g., SEC-USA, FCA-UK) for enforcement cooperation
UPSC trap: IOSCO membership gives SEBI soft-law obligations — not legally binding, but India must align regulations to maintain credibility

concepts.name: Recent SEBI Reforms: Finfluencer Regulation and Algo Trading
key_dimensions: Finfluencer regulation (2024): Unregistered persons barred from giving securities advice; platforms must ensure compliance
Algorithmic (Algo) trading regulation: API-based retail algo trading brought under SEBI framework
T+1 settlement cycle: India became one of the first major markets to implement T+1 — reduces counterparty risk
UPSC trap: T+0 settlement pilot launched in 2024 — India's leadership in settlement innovation is a positive example in economy questions

concepts.name: SEBI's Funding Mechanism and Financial Autonomy
key_dimensions: SEBI funded through fees charged on market participants (registration fees, transaction charges) — NOT through parliamentary appropriation
This financial independence is key to regulatory autonomy — contrast with ministries
SEBI must maintain a reserve fund; surplus transferred to Consolidated Fund of India after board decision
UPSC trap: SEBI's financial autonomy does NOT mean full independence — government appoints Chairman and nominees sit on board, creating accountability tension
